body:
If you switch to Jolt Physics (Project / Project Settings... / Physics / 3D / Physics Engine / Jolt Physics) it works much better. In my experience the GodotPhysics soft body implementation has the tendency to explode.

Note that beyond setting the 'Pressure Coefficient' (try 100-1000) you don't have a lot of options to try to preserve the volume of these soft bodies. Pressure works with the box, but it doesn't work with the monkey as the mesh is not closed. For better volume preservation, Jolt's [tetrahedral volume constraints](https://github.com/jrouwe/JoltPhysics/blob/390cefd44c7625b16f259e8954af65809144d9bc/Jolt/Physics/SoftBody/SoftBodySharedSettings.h#L207-L222) would need to be exposed in godot.
https://github.com/godotengine/godot-docs/pull/11423 updates the soft body documentation to add a Jolt Physics recommendation.

Using Jolt works a lot better.  The meshes still collapse into puddles, though, even if I use a pressure coefficient of 1000.  

I edited the monkey mesh so now it is a manifold without holes:

[soft-body-test.zip](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/23181105/soft-body-test.zip)

>  The meshes still collapse into puddles

You probably need to set Linear Coefficient to a higher value. Note that I've noticed that in general, soft body simulation can behave very differently according to the **Physics Ticks per Second** project setting. Higher values are not always more stable or consistent either.

Increasing the Linear Coefficient that helped keep the cube rigid, but the monkey still collapses.  Preserving the tetrahedral volume sounds like it could be useful, so I'd be in favour of exposing it in the editor.  

Here's an example with Jolt showing the monkey holding it's shape much better:
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=MksMh-3RFYw

I would say that that video uses more than just the edges of the mesh to keep the shape (which is the only thing possible in godot). Could be extra internal edges or tetrahedrons.

I would say: Create a proposal for this.

Okay.  I'm not that familiar with Jolt.  Would you know how to use the Jolt API to set up a tetrahedral volume based simulation?  It's not obvious to me how that  would be done looking at their doc webpage.

Here's a very simple example: https://github.com/jrouwe/JoltPhysics/blob/4ba006783baaa089397a95f324616bfea54b1b61/Jolt/Physics/SoftBody/SoftBodySharedSettings.cpp#L1390-L1412

The trick is to figure out which tetrahedrons to create. Usually you create a low resolution representation of your model that you make out of tetrahedrons and then map the simulated results onto your higher resolution mesh. E.g. through https://github.com/wildmeshing/fTetWild or https://gmsh.info/.

I started hacking on this over the break.  I've gotten to the point where I can start building the tetrahedra tessellation.  gmsh looks huge and even fTetWild has a lot of files in it.  I could try adding fTetWild to the Godot code base (MPL-2.0 license), although I know from a different issue (about EXR files) that the Godot project is cautious about code bloat.  Should I add them?

Alternately, I could try rolling my own tessellation algorithm.  Or are either of the libraries @jrouwe mentioned already in the code base?  I searched, but could not find them.

Edit:

After reading up on the fTetWild algorithm, it's the best choice IMHO.  It's pretty clever and the simple grid based tessellation I had in mind is pretty inferior to it.

fTetWild appears to have a dependency on a library called Eigen (https://libeigen.gitlab.io/), which itself is pretty big.  I might need some advice for including these libraries in the Godot source.

Those libraries are indeed not in the third_party folder yet. I just gave them as examples. Closest thing that is available is vhacd. This library decomposes meshes into convex hulls which would make creating tetrahedrons easy. Unfortunately, you'll need to connect the tetrahedrons between the different convex parts, which is not much simpler than the original problem (and since the generated convex hulls can overlap not always possible).

> ... that the Godot project is cautious about code bloat. Should I add them?

Not really my call, but Eigen seems like quite a lot to pull in.

Eigen is huge, but fTetWild seems to only be using the vector and dense matrix objects in it.  Maybe it could be rewritten so it doesn't require such a huge dependency?

The fTetWild algorithm looks like a really good approach, so I'd prefer to use it if I could.  But using convex hulls would probably take much less code.

Are there any good summaries of all the different third party libraries in the code base?

Edit:
Tetgen looks like it could be a good solution.  It's not as robust as fTetWild, but is pretty small and has no 3rd party dependencies. https://wias-berlin.de/software/index.jsp?id=TetGen&lang=1
I can't help you with these questions. I maintain Jolt, not godot.
I was hoping @Calinou would reply since he seems to be the one who would know these things.

I was away on Christmas break, but I'm getting combing through the notification backlog as I'm writing this 🙂

> 
> [ufz/tetgen](https://github.com/ufz/tetgen?rgh-link-date=2026-01-04T03%3A00%3A08.000Z)

Using AGPL-licensed code is not possible in Godot as per the [copyright guidelines](https://contributing.godotengine.org/en/latest/organization/general_rules_and_guidelines.html#respect-copyright).

MPL-licensed code is fine, but I consider having to link against Eigen a dealbreaker due to its size and buildsystem complexity.

Okay.  Most of the libraries out there are GPL family or have huge dependencies.  I might need to write my own.  

How do you add new source files to the project?  Third party or otherwise?

Does Godot have an octree library?  All I can find is one that seems to be exclusive to the GI code.

> How do you add new source files to the project? Third party or otherwise?

Libraries have to be integrated using SCons. We don't reuse the library's original build system (typically CMake). There isn't dedicated documentation for this, but you can check existing libraries in the [`thirdparty/`](https://github.com/godotengine/godot/tree/master/thirdparty) folder for an example. You can take inspiration from [enet](https://github.com/godotengine/godot/tree/master/thirdparty/enet), which is a good starting point for a library that needs to be built on its own, with only certain files compiled. Any code changes made to the library should be made in the form of `.patch` files, so that they can be reapplied during library upgrades.[^1]

[^1]: To clarify, the library files should already be patched, but you should keep the `.patch` files in version control. SCons won't use the `.patch` files at build-time.

Outside of third-party code, there is no need to explicitly state source files to be added to the project in SCons files. Create a new source file, `#include` it and you are ready to go. For third-party libraries, globs can also be used to include all files in the folder (see [minizip](https://github.com/godotengine/godot/blob/8dcf5b4eafff013b7d7022c5c1b3e33dc15e5947/modules/zip/SCsub) as an example).

> Does Godot have an octree library? All I can find is one that seems to be exclusive to the GI code.

Godot used to have its own octree for culling purposes, but it was replaced by a BVH in the 3.x days. The octree code was removed, so you'll have to find an octree library that's lightweight enough to be integrated in Godot.

I spent some time writing my own tetrahedralizer library: https://github.com/blackears/cyclops_tetrahedralizer

I'm using cmake to build it, since that also allows me to create a standalone app with it.  It has no dependencies.

How do I create a `.patch` file?  Do I just copy the relevant files into `/thirdparty/cyclopsTetrahedralizer`, make the necessary changes, make a diff with my source repo and then put a copy of the `.patch` under `/thirdparty/cyclopsTetrahedralizer/patches`?

Also, where do I set up the scons build process?  `/thirdparty/enet` doesn't seem to have any build file in it.

> How do I create a .patch file? Do I just copy the relevant files into /thirdparty/cyclopsTetrahedralizer, make the necessary changes, make a diff with my source repo and then put a copy of the .patch under /thirdparty/cyclopsTetrahedralizer/patches?

That should be it, yes. File paths in `.patch` files should match the Godot directory structure; see [`thirdparty/sdl/patches/0003-std-include.patch`](https://github.com/godotengine/godot/blob/master/thirdparty/sdl/patches/0003-std-include.patch) for an example.

> Also, where do I set up the scons build process? `/thirdparty/enet` doesn't seem to have any build file in it.

The build process is set up in your module, rather than in the thirdparty folder. Check `modules/enet/SCsub` for an example.

Looks like Godot already has a delunay tetrahedralizer in it called Delunay3D.  Wish I'd seen that earlier.  I'll try using that instead.

@jrouwe, when I build the SoftBodySharedSettings, should I add edges and faces once, or should I add them going both ways?  That is, if two tetrahedra have an edge from v[0] to v[1], should I only add the edge [0, 1], or do I need to add both [0, 1] and [1, 0]?  Same if one has the face [0, 1, 2] and the second shares the face but has vertices [0, 2, 1].

From the code in SoftBodySharedSettings::sCreateCube, it looks like I only need one, but want to confirm because the Jolt docs don't seem to say.

Also, for the tetrahedra, should the volumes have positive or negative determinants?  Or does it matter? (Ie, if the faces were using a right handed winding, would the normals point to the interior or exterior of the tetrahedron?)

Edges should be added once, faces I would only add on the exterior (only used for collision detection). Volumes, I don't think it matters but to be safe I would go for positive determinants (faces are assumed counter clockwise).

@Calinou, does Godot have anything I could use to cast a ray from inside a mesh and determine if it hits a mesh face and if so, the normal of that face?  I'm thinking of adding code for a bvh tree for doing this test, but wasn't sure if something like that might already be in the code base.  There is a bvh tree, but that seems to be more for node objects than doing ray-triangle intersection tests.

> [@Calinou](https://github.com/Calinou), does Godot have anything I could use to cast a ray from inside a mesh and determine if it hits a mesh face and if so, the normal of that face?

Not yet, but https://github.com/godotengine/godot/pull/115593 implements this.

Okay, I think I got it.  I noticed when I rebased my simulation got significantly stiffer.  Is there any way to set the floppiness of the SoftBodySharedSettings?  Just setting the stiffness doesn't seem to do much.

> I noticed when I rebased my simulation got significantly stiffer.

Yes we 'fixed' the conversion of stiffness to compliance in #116041.

> Is there any way to set the floppiness of the SoftBodySharedSettings

Compliance is the only parameter that you can tweak. You can have different compliance settings for volume constraints vs edge constraints though (and it's probably smart to do that).
